original_question: For the inhomogeneous Boltzmann equation with a physically meaningful collision kernel, do global classical solutions exist for generic initial data? This is the unconditional global well posedness problem outside perturbative or near-equilibrium regimes.
target_in_paper: Section 3, item (3) "Unconditional global well posedness" for the inhomogeneous Boltzmann equation, sharpened in Section 8.1 ("Unconditional regularity estimates") as the problem of proving the hydrodynamic bounds (3.1)-(3.3), which by Theorem 3.1 would imply global smooth solutions.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the inhomogeneous Boltzmann equation, the nonperturbative/global-in-time classical-solvability issue, and the fact that the question is about unconditional global well posedness rather than the near-equilibrium theory. It also matches the paper's contrast between perturbative results and the much harder problem for generic initial data.
missing_details: The exact Cauchy problem should be stated: partial_t f + v . grad_x f = Q(f,f), with f(0,x,v) = f_in(x,v).
The paper's concrete conditional regularity theorem is stated in the periodic spatial setting x in T^d, with velocity variable v in R^d.
The relevant unknown is a nonnegative classical/smooth solution f = f(t,x,v), not merely a weak or renormalized solution.
The collision kernel should be narrowed from "physically meaningful" to the standard non-cutoff inverse-power-law Boltzmann kernel discussed in Section 2.1, rather than an unspecified broad class.
The draft leaves the functional setting for "generic initial data" implicit; the paper phrases this as initial data in some natural space for which a short-time classical theory is available.
The paper's sharper Section 8.1 formulation is not just "do global smooth solutions exist?" but "can one prove the hydrodynamic bounds (3.1), (3.2), (3.3)?"
Those hydrodynamic bounds should be spelled out pointwise in (t,x): lower and upper mass density, upper energy density, and upper entropy density.
The needed quantifiers are missing: the bounds are to hold for every (t,x), hence for all t >= 0 and all spatial points x.
The draft does not say that Theorem 3.1 supplies only an implication: if the hydrodynamic bounds hold, then smoothness persists; the paper does not prove an equivalence.
The draft does not reflect the paper's focus on singularity formation from smooth data and the possibility that uniqueness could fail past a singularity.
refined_question: For the Cauchy problem for the inhomogeneous Boltzmann equation on [0,infinity) x T^d_x x R^d_v, partial_t f + v . grad_x f = Q(f,f), f(0,x,v) = f_in(x,v) >= 0, with Q the standard non-cutoff Boltzmann collision operator for inverse-power-law interactions (so the collision kernel has the form B(|v-v_*|, cos theta) = |v-v_*|^gamma b(cos theta), with a nonintegrable angular singularity of the usual physical type), can one prove that every smooth initial datum f_in in a class admitting short-time classical solvability gives rise to a global-in-time smooth solution, without any smallness assumption near a Maxwellian or near vacuum? More concretely, can one establish constants m_0, M_0, E_0, H_0 such that for all t >= 0 and x in T^d one has 0 < m_0 <= integral_{R^d} f(t,x,v) dv <= M_0, integral_{R^d} |v|^2 f(t,x,v) dv <= E_0, and integral_{R^d} f(t,x,v) log f(t,x,v) dv <= H_0, which Theorem 3.1 would then turn into global smoothness?
justification: This paper does not package the target as a numbered conjecture; the closest official formulation is the Section 3 description of "unconditional global well posedness" for the inhomogeneous Boltzmann equation, together with the more concrete Section 8.1 question of whether the hydrodynamic bounds (3.1)-(3.3) can be proved. Your draft captures the broad aim, but it is still looser than the paper in three ways: it does not specify the Cauchy problem or the paper's non-cutoff kernel framework, it leaves the functional setting and spatial domain implicit, and it omits the paper's key reformulation through hydrodynamic bounds, which is the precise mechanism singled out as sufficient for global smoothness via Theorem 3.1.
